St. Ignatius of Antioch

Ignatius the God-Bearer · Ignatios

What is depictedHistory and traditionPublished explanationSources

Mikhail Dikarev’s 1894 icon presents Ignatius as a bishop, with lions shown beside him. The file identifies the Hermitage collection and its inventory number.

[1] Displayed work;file-level title,description,date and visual identification

What is depicted

The bishop stands in an open landscape, holding a book and blessing. Two lions appear at his feet; Christ is shown above. The scene combines the hierarch’s portrait with his martyrdom tradition rather than depicting a modern ecclesiastical official.

[1] Displayed work;file-level title,description,date and visual identification

History and tradition

The panel is catalogued as Dikarev’s 1894 Ignatius the God-Bearer, Hermitage inventoryЭРЖ-2513. The letter excerpt is an earlier primary Christian voice in a specified 1885 English translation. The author addresses Roman Christians concerning his approaching martyrdom; the passage is not a prayer rule created for this app.

[1] Displayed work;file-level title,description,date and visual identification

Published explanation

I write to the Churches, and impress on them all, that I shall willingly die for God, unless ye hinder me. I beseech of you not to show an unseasonable good-will towards me. Suffer me to become food for the wild beasts, through whose instrumentality it will be granted me to attain to God. I am the wheat of God, and let me be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ. Rather entice the wild beasts, that they may become my tomb, and may leave nothing of my body; so that when I have fallen asleep [in death], I may be no trouble to any one. Then shall I truly be a disciple of Christ, when the world shall not see so much as my body. Entreat Christ for me, that by these instruments I may be found a sacrifice [to God]. I do not, as Peter and Paul, issue commandments unto you. They were apostles; I am but a condemned man: they were free, while I am, even until now, a servant. But when I suffer, I shall be the freed-man of Jesus, and shall rise again emancipated in Him. And now, being a prisoner, I learn not to desire anything worldly or vain.

Ignatius’s own letter,shorter recension,in the Roberts and Donaldson translation printed in Ante-Nicene Fathersvol1,American edition1885. The adjacent longer recension is not spliced into this text.

[2] Epistle to the RomansIV,shorter recension
